title: Design a File Storage Service
brief: People store files online, open them from any device, and edit them together. Downloads are most of the traffic, uploads are rarer but heavy, and two people saving the same file at once must not overwrite each other. Other devices are told when a file changes, and uploaded images get preview thumbnails made in the background.
constraints: Opening or downloading a file must start within 200 ms
About 10,000 file requests per second at peak, and about 1 in 12 is an upload
Two people saving the same file at once must never silently overwrite each other
Other devices learn about a change within a second, but the service works without that
Thumbnails are generated in the background after an upload

capabilities.label: Download a file
capabilities.hint: Find a file and stream its contents to the user

capabilities.label: Save a file or a new version
capabilities.hint: Store the contents and record the new version. Two saves of the same file at once must not both win.

capabilities.label: Notify other devices
capabilities.hint: Tell a user's other devices that a file changed, over a live connection

capabilities.label: Make previews
capabilities.hint: Create small preview images for newly uploaded pictures, about 3% of requests

scenarios.title: Typical peak
scenarios.description: Steady downloads with the usual share of uploads.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Downloads and uploads stress different things. How do you keep a big upload from slowing everyone's downloads?
scenarios.debrief: The CDN serves most downloads, so storage sees only misses and uploads.

scenarios.title: Monday morning (3x)
scenarios.description: Everyone opens their files at once and traffic triples.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Most of the extra load is downloads of popular files. What absorbs it before it reaches storage?
scenarios.debrief: Popular files are the same few objects, which the CDN holds. Autoscaling covers the rest.

scenarios.title: Storage slows down (3x)
scenarios.interviewQuestion: File storage is slow. Which downloads can still be fast, and what makes that possible?
scenarios.debrief: Most downloads never reach storage, so a 3x slower store only shows in the miss path.

scenarios.title: Live notifications hang
scenarios.description: Whatever runs device notifications becomes 20x slower.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Notifications hang instead of failing cleanly. Should opening or saving a file wait for them, and where does the notification code live?
scenarios.debrief: Notifications are in their own server behind the breaker, so a hang there never reaches a download.

requirements.text: Downloads start within the latency target at peak
Downloads are served through a CDN in front of storage
Something saves files, and never lets two saves silently overwrite each other
Files stay usable when live notifications hang
The design explains how conflicting edits are detected and what the user sees

rubric: Files live in blob storage; a database holds only metadata and versions.
A CDN serves popular downloads so storage sees a fraction of the load.
Saving a version is protected by a lock or a version check so concurrent saves are detected.
Previews are made by workers off the upload path, from a queue.
Device notifications use live connections but the service does not depend on them.

reference.summary: Serve downloads through a CDN, protect version writes with locks, and keep notifications and previews out of the main path.
design: User, then a CDN (93% hit), then a Load Balancer, then an App Server (8 replicas, autoscale to 24) running 'Download a file' and 'Save a file or a new version'.
The App Server reads Blob Storage for contents and a document Database (Row locks, read replica) for versions.
Device notifications run in a separate WebSocket Server, called behind the app server's circuit breaker.
Previews: the App Server sends work to a Queue asynchronously, and Workers make thumbnails.
tradeoffs: The separate notification server costs a little and keeps a hung connection from slowing downloads.
Row locks on version writes prevent silent overwrites at a small write-throughput cost.
